models.inverse_notes: A = S - B and B = S - A given the other input; both respect the original (empty) guard set. Substitution: S = 10500, B = 1500 gives A = 9000, and forward 9000 + 1500 = 10500. Single-output vs many-inputs: S alone underdetermines (A, B) - infinitely many pairs sum to S (e.g. S = 10500 admits both (9000, 1500) and (10000, 500)) - so the output cannot be inverted to named components, which is why sum_of_money stays a distinct meaning from named_money_amount (brief 19). Boundary S = 0 with A = 0 gives B = 0 uniquely; S = 0 with A = 5 gives B = -5 under the signed admission.
limitations: No currency conversion: amounts in other currencies must be translated to USD externally (ASC 830) before entry; this record never converts.

Two inputs only: three-or-more-component and family aggregates are separate relationships, deferred, not implied by repeated application (SUM-orientation: the sum output cannot re-enter as a named input).
Signed arithmetic is admitted; the record does not enforce nonnegativity or balance-sheet sign conventions.

New quantity meaning counted_unit_quantity (dimensionless) for the item-count input.
New glue context for same-lot USD valuation and count basis.
Output meaning unit_price exists in the registry vocabulary; its 6 consumer contexts were read on 2026-11-04 and none equals this record output context, so this record binds no existing consumer.

models.inverse_notes: T = R x Q given R and Q; Q = T / R requires R nonzero; both must re-satisfy T >= 0 and Q > 0. Substitution: R = 95, Q = 500 gives T = 47500, and forward 47500 / 500 = 95. R = 0 with T = 0 leaves Q underdetermined (any positive count fits); R = 0 with T > 0 is impossible. Recovered counts need not be integers: fractional Q is arithmetic only and carries no item-fraction semantics.
limitations: Counts only: gallon, ounce, pound, kilowatthour and other physical-measure quantities are excluded and rejected (rejection case); they never enter counted_unit_quantity.
Identical items required: mixed lots need separate rates per homogeneous group, not one blended rate.

Not average production cost (see economics--average-total-production-cost: units produced, TC/Q) nor the family-weighted transaction mean (see economics--identical-product-mean-transaction-price); this record is the single-lot scalar transaction rate.

references.method: Regulation fact pattern with an independently derived total: 19 CFR 152.105 note 2 publishes 500 units at $95 (and 400 at $90); the extended total $47,500 is derived by multiplication, and the record division recovers the published $95 unit price. Boundary: a zero-total (free) lot rates at zero per item, pinning the T = 0 boundary admitted by T >= 0. Curator-constructed boundary, not a published figure.

rejection_cases.reason: Q = 0 violates Q > 0 (division undefined). Gallon, ounce and other physical-measure quantities are likewise excluded: they never enter the counted_unit_quantity meaning, so a volume-denominated value fails closed at composition on meaning/unit mismatch rather than entering this division.

T is omitted: without the named lot total no rate is computable. A sum_of_money output cannot substitute for the named_money_amount total (SUM-orientation: input and output meanings stay distinct); the composition fails closed.

relationship.original_equation: R = T / Q (lot total divided by counted identical items)
relationship.translation_notes: T is the introduced lot total; Q is the introduced item count; R is the introduced unit rate. Dimensional check: currency / 1 = currency per unit on the shared USD basis. BLS converts collected prices to a price per normalized quantity and CBP apportions totals over numbers of units; this record applies that per-quantity shape to counted identical items as the conservative restriction documented in brief 19 (BLS practice also spans physical measures; this record admits counts only).

sources.evidence: The Handbook states that all eligible prices are converted to a price per normalized quantity (flour per ounce averaged, times 16 for the published price per pound); that combined apple weight is divided by 2 and the 50-cent apple price divided by the average weight; and the quantity-discount fact pattern: a 12-ounce can of corn at 25 cents single, three cans for 69 cents, or five cans for $1, priced per ounce from the three-can offer. Per-can rates derive from the same figures by count division.
